source.title: TableOS System Design — as built
source.notice: Based on the uploaded 9-page PDF. Deployed-system facts are attributed to the document's 19 Nov 2026 snapshot. Teaching examples are illustrations, not independently verified system behavior.

modules.title: 1. What TableOS Is
modules.overview: Understand the product and its hierarchy before diving into infrastructure. This section describes the source's deployed v0.36.0 snapshot, not a promise about later releases.

terms.definition: A team-oriented, Airtable-style relational database platform.
terms.example: A sales team manages Leads and Deals in tables.
terms.use: Lets teams configure data and processes without changing backend schemas.

terms.definition: Top-level tenant containing members and workspaces.
terms.example: Blue Cascade is the tenant; teams work inside it.

terms.definition: Container grouping related bases inside an organization.
terms.example: Sales workspace has CRM and Reporting bases.

terms.definition: A database-like project containing tables, views and automations.
terms.example: CRM base contains Leads and Deals.
terms.use: Unit of data changes and realtime subscriptions.

terms.definition: Collection of records with fields.
terms.use: Stores one category of structured business data.

terms.definition: A row containing field values.
terms.use: CRUD target in the REST API.

terms.definition: Typed column describing a record attribute.
Saved presentation/query of a table.
terms.example: Kanban grouped by status or calendar by date.
terms.use: Different UIs over the same underlying records.

terms.definition: A page-based app assembled over data from a base.
terms.use: Task-specific frontend without exposing the raw grid.

terms.definition: A trigger followed by actions.
terms.example: When a new lead is created, send a message.

terms.definition: A table populated by another data source.
terms.example: HubSpot contacts copied into a TableOS table.
terms.use: Connect external CRM or another base.

terms.definition: Token-authenticated REST access to platform resources.

flow: Organization contains workspaces.
Workspace contains one or more bases.
Base contains tables; tables contain fields and records.
Views present those records in grid, gallery, kanban, calendar, timeline, list, Gantt or form.
Automations, interfaces, comments, syncs, attachments and sharing operate around that data.
modules.example: Learning example: A support organization creates a Support workspace → Tickets base → Tickets table → Status and Priority fields → Kanban view. This illustrates the documented hierarchy; the PDF does not assert that this specific base exists.

questions.prompt: What is the correct TableOS hierarchy?
questions.why: An organization groups workspaces; workspaces group bases; bases contain tables and records.

questions.prompt: Which feature changes how records appear without creating another table?
questions.why: Views display the same table in different layouts and with saved filtering/grouping.

questions.prompt: An application needs to create records from an external script. Which interface is intended?
options: Public REST API with access token
questions.why: The document explicitly lists a public REST API accessed with tokens.

modules.remember: Remember: TableOS is a data platform with a hierarchy plus workflows and integrations—not just a spreadsheet.

modules.title: 2. Deployment Topology
modules.overview: Trace each service in the deployed architecture. The source specifies Render Singapore for compute/database/cache and Google Cloud Storage for objects.

terms.definition: The Fastify-backed service handling HTTP requests and several schedulers.
WebSocket gateway transmitting changes and presence.
terms.example: A colleague sees a cell update.

terms.definition: Background process consuming BullMQ jobs and domain events.
Process polling database outbox rows and publishing events.
Relational system storing core, data and audit tables.
In-memory datastore used for queues, event bus, locks and realtime fan-out.
terms.example: Publish a base change to subscribers.

terms.definition: Object storage for private attachments and thumbnails.
Built React application delivered as static assets.
Separate app serving shared views, forms and interfaces.
terms.example: Anyone with a valid share link submits a form.

terms.definition: Observability platform for dashboards and monitoring.
Versioned database schema change.
terms.use: Keep deployed schema compatible with app code.

flow: Browser uses HTTPS to communicate with the API and WSS to the realtime gateway.
API validates permissions and writes to Postgres.
Worker processes queued and event-triggered work, with Redis/Valkey assisting coordination.
Relay moves committed outbox events to the event bus.
Attachments live in private GCS; authorized clients access short-lived links.
Grafana and structured logs provide operational visibility.
modules.example: As built (19 Nov 2026): API web service 2 CPU/4 GB; realtime 1 CPU/2 GB; worker 1 CPU/2 GB; relay 0.5 CPU/512 MB. A single Postgres 18 database and Valkey 8 instance are shared; the original sharded/Kafka-style target design is not deployed.

questions.prompt: Which component polls outbox_events and publishes to the Redis event bus?
questions.why: The relay bridges committed PostgreSQL outbox records to the Redis event bus.

questions.prompt: Why store attachments in GCS instead of in the relational records table?
options: To separate large binary objects from structured data
questions.why: Object storage handles large files; PostgreSQL stores the structured metadata.

questions.prompt: Does the deployed design already use the original sharded data plane and Kafka-style log?
options: No; the document says those belong to the target design
questions.why: The PDF explicitly distinguishes as-built single Postgres/Redis deployment from original target architecture.

modules.remember: Remember: API, realtime, worker and relay are separate runtime responsibilities around a single Postgres and Redis-compatible store.

modules.title: 3. Code Structure and Libraries
modules.overview: Follow the TypeScript monorepo. The same server codebase has separate entrypoints; shared packages provide reusable domain logic.

terms.definition: Repository containing multiple apps and shared packages.
terms.example: apps/server and apps/web in one repo.

terms.definition: JavaScript package manager supporting monorepo workspaces.
Build orchestration tool for monorepos.
Program start target for a given runtime role.
terms.use: Run distinct services from one codebase.

terms.definition: Node.js HTTP framework used by server code.
Type-safe TypeScript SQL query builder.
PostgreSQL client for Node.js.
Redis-backed Node.js job queue library.
Redis/Valkey client for Node.js.
Runtime schema parsing and validation library.
Frontend component library and build tool.
Client-side management for server state.
Small client state store.

flow: apps/server contains API, realtime, worker and relay code; scheduler is listed as a stub entrypoint.
apps/web builds authenticated React SPA; apps/public builds no-account shared-view and form app.
packages/fields defines codecs and validation; formula and compute packages handle calculated values.
packages/db supplies migrations and typed SQL; packages/auth and permissions enforce access.
packages/events/jobs/realtime-protocol/connectors share contracts across services.
modules.example: Learning example: A new Currency field involves a codec in packages/fields, a cell editor in packages/field-ui, query handling in packages/query, and API validation in apps/server. This example follows the documented boundaries; it is not an asserted change log entry.

questions.prompt: Where does the PDF locate shared field-type codecs?
questions.why: The source names packages/fields for 31 field types, codecs and validation.

questions.prompt: What advantage comes from separate api and worker entrypoints in one codebase?
options: All jobs must share one process
Shared domain code with independently deployed runtime roles
questions.why: One codebase can reuse contracts while runtime roles are started separately.

questions.prompt: Why must API input still be validated with Zod even if TypeScript types exist?
options: Types run on untrusted JSON automatically
TypeScript types do not enforce runtime input shapes
questions.why: Types disappear at runtime; parsing/validation protects API boundaries.

modules.remember: Remember: different apps and services share types, but each running process has a separate responsibility.

modules.title: 4. Data Model and Record Storage
modules.overview: Understand the three PostgreSQL schemas and why adding fields does not require new SQL columns.

terms.definition: PostgreSQL namespace for identity, tenancy, access and integrations.
Namespace for bases, tables, records, history, syncs and automations.
Namespace for security-relevant activity events.
PostgreSQL binary JSON representation with query operators.
Internal immutable key identifying a field's stored value.
terms.example: cells keyed by slot, not display label.
terms.use: Rename fields without changing data keys.

terms.definition: Derived values stored separately from user-edited cells.
Table storing relationships between records.
Auxiliary rows indexing typed values from flexible JSONB records.
Database definition changes such as ALTER TABLE.
terms.use: Avoided for normal user field edits.

terms.definition: Identifier with a type-specific prefix.
Per-base ordered counter for data changes.
Saved snapshot/change record for history.

flow: Metadata about table fields is saved in data.fields.
Editable cell values are keyed by stable slots in data.records.cells JSONB.
Computed formula/lookup/rollup results are persisted in data.records.computed.
Linked-record relationships live in data.record_links.
Large tables can use numeric/text/time sidecars for indexed sorts and filters.
Adding/deleting a user field changes metadata rather than altering database table columns.
modules.example: Illustrative storage: {cells:{'slot_a':'Ali','slot_b':1200},computed:{'slot_total':2400}}. Slots are invented for teaching, not real TableOS slot IDs. The source records 79 PostgreSQL tables across core, data and audit.

questions.prompt: Where do ordinary record values reside?
options: data.records.cells JSONB keyed by stable slots
One SQL column per user field
questions.why: The source explicitly places editable values under stable slot keys in JSONB.

questions.prompt: Why can a user add a field without a SQL ALTER TABLE?
options: Field metadata and JSONB slots represent dynamic fields
questions.why: Dynamic field definitions avoid modifying the physical schema for every user column.

questions.prompt: How are numeric/date filters accelerated on large flexible tables?
questions.why: The source describes record_index_num/text/time sidecars.

modules.remember: Remember: meta schema is stable; flexible user-defined fields live in JSONB and sidecar indexes.

modules.title: 5. A Change, End to End
modules.overview: Follow the core system-design interview story: one authenticated record update becomes a durable transaction, a realtime frame and downstream event.

terms.definition: Request middleware verifying a session or API token.
Compiled effective actions for a user and base.
Permission check for a specific action.
TableOS transaction wrapper around one base mutation.
terms.example: Update a cell and its revision.

terms.definition: Monotonic per-base sequence of changes.
Event rows written in the same DB transaction as business changes.
Persisted per-base change frames.
Logic executed only once transaction succeeds.
SQL locking option letting concurrent workers claim distinct rows.
Fact indicating a meaningful change.
Browser displays an edit before server confirmation.

flow: 1. Browser sends PATCH/POST with session cookie or bearer token.
2. Auth hook applies MFA/device conditions; compileForUser computes access; assertCan checks action and field rules.
3. withBaseTx increments change_seq, writes cells and revisions, runs dependent compute and queues sync pushes.
4. In the SAME transaction, append data.base_changes and data.outbox_events.
5. Commit succeeds. Only then publish realtime frame to a base Redis channel; other tabs patch caches.
6. Relay reads outbox with locking and publishes domain events; workers update search, send notifications and trigger syncs/automations.
modules.example: Learning trace: A user edits Ticket Status from Open to Resolved. The database update, revision, sequence increment and outbox event either all commit together or all roll back. The UI publishes the new status only after commit. Exact schema identifiers and example field names are illustrative.

questions.prompt: What must be in the same transaction as a record update?
options: Revision, base change and outbox event
questions.why: The source's one-transaction design atomically stores mutation, revision, base_changes and outbox.

questions.prompt: Why publish realtime updates only after COMMIT?
options: To avoid announcing a change that might roll back
questions.why: Clients should not observe a change that was not durably committed.

questions.prompt: What failure does the transactional outbox help prevent?
options: Committed DB change with no downstream event publication
questions.why: Persist the event with the business change; relay can publish later.

modules.remember: Remember this 6-step explanation; it is the most important TableOS system-design interview flow.

modules.title: 6. Realtime and Presence
modules.overview: Understand collaboration, synchronization after gaps and why WebSocket tickets are separate from normal API sessions.

terms.definition: Persistent bidirectional browser-server connection.
Short-lived proof allowing an authenticated client to connect.
Named application protocol on top of WebSocket.
Gateway subscription to events for one base.
Periodic signal describing active user location.
Resend ordered changes after a client's last known number.
Signal asking a client to refetch when a gap cannot be replayed.
Client identifier for a particular optimistic edit.
Immediate authorization change broadcast.
Distribution of base changes across realtime gateways.
terms.example: One gateway forwards to connected users.

flow: 1. Authenticated client requests a short-lived WebSocket ticket.
2. Browser connects using tableos.v1 and subscribes to a base, optionally supplying last sequence.
3. Gateway delivers change frames and presence lists, with Redis subscription per base.
4. Collaborators see avatars and selected cells; clients send presence heartbeats.
5. If a sequence gap is recoverable, replay; otherwise emit resync_required.
6. Removed access is signaled immediately so connected tabs disconnect from the base.
modules.example: Learning scenario: Editor A updates a cell while Editor B is viewing it. B receives a frame and patches the cached row without requesting the entire grid. A ignores the matching own-mutation frame. This follows the documented browser behavior.

questions.prompt: What does a realtime client request before opening the TableOS WebSocket?
options: A public API key pasted in UI
questions.why: The source states POST /v1/auth/ws-ticket precedes connection.

questions.prompt: What should a client do when the server sends resync_required?
questions.why: It signals a gap that cannot be safely replayed.

questions.prompt: Why does a browser ignore a frame with its own client mutation ID?
options: To avoid reapplying an optimistic local edit
questions.why: The sender has already applied its optimistic change and can suppress duplicate presentation.

modules.remember: Remember: WebSocket sends changes, sequence numbers preserve order, presence is ephemeral, and DB remains source of truth.

modules.title: 7. Background Work and Event Bus
modules.overview: Separate queued jobs, domain events, relay and scheduled jobs—four concepts interviewers often mix up.

terms.definition: Named Redis-backed work list consumed by workers.
Code adding jobs for later execution.
Worker processing a job.
Subscriber handling committed platform facts.
Worker claiming unpublished DB events and forwarding to bus.
Time between relay checks.
Task initiated at configured times.
Mutual exclusion coordination across worker processes.
terms.example: One sync run at a time.

terms.definition: Worker maintaining searchable text.
Runner for triggers, schedules and steps.

flow: API transaction writes outbox_events; it does not synchronously execute every downstream effect.
Relay polls roughly every 0.5 s and claims batches of 50 using database row locks.
Redis event bus delivers events to consumers such as search-indexer, collaboration notifications and table-sync.
BullMQ worker processes compute, automation-trigger/step, webhook-out, email, notification, search-index, file-scan/process, import/export, AI, sync, snapshot, purge and maintenance queues.
API schedulers also run sync sweeps, HubSpot push/mapping, retention, trash purge and time formulas.
Database locks protect scheduled syncs from simultaneous API/worker execution.
modules.example: Learning example: An uploaded CSV creates an import job. The HTTP request can return quickly, a worker imports rows later, and events trigger search indexing. The exact queue and table names follow the source; the example sequence is illustrative.

questions.prompt: Which library backs TableOS background queues?
questions.why: The source lists BullMQ on Redis/Valkey for many job types.

questions.prompt: Why use FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED when claiming outbox events?
options: Allow several relays to claim distinct rows
questions.why: Skip locked rows prevents concurrent claimers waiting on already claimed rows.

questions.prompt: Two schedulers try to sync the same source. What mechanism is documented?
questions.why: A DB lock guards scheduler runs to avoid concurrent duplicate sync operations.

modules.remember: Remember: jobs are work requests; events describe things that happened; schedulers start work by time.

modules.title: 8. Fields, Formulas and Compute
modules.overview: Learn the field engine: typed validation, dependency tracking, calculated values and sensitive-data policies.

terms.definition: Kind of value and available operations.
Rules for parsing, serializing and converting a type.
Expression computed from record data.
Converts formula text into a structured typed representation.
Tree of expression nodes annotated with types.
Read a field through a linked record.
Aggregate linked records.
Computed number of related records.
terms.example: Number of tickets for a customer.

terms.definition: Map of fields that depend on other fields.
terms.example: Total depends on Quantity and Price.

terms.definition: Recalculate only affected derived values.
Time-dependent formula functions refreshed by a scheduler.
Hiding protected values unless reveal policy permits access.
Allowed people who may reveal selected sensitive fields.

flow: User creates a typed field; field package supplies codec, validation, filtering, sorting and conversions.
When a formula is saved, parser/evaluator identifies dependencies.
A changed input cell causes server runCompute to refresh affected formulas, lookups, rollups or counts.
Time-dependent expressions refresh on schedule because time can change without edits.
Email, Phone and Sensitive-marked fields are masked unless an authorized user reveals one cell with a logged reason.
modules.example: Learning example: Line Item has Quantity 3, Unit Price 20; formula Total = Quantity * Unit Price yields 60. Change Quantity to 4; dependency graph triggers recompute to 80. Expression is illustrative; incremental computation is documented.

questions.prompt: What enables efficient recomputation after one input field changes?
questions.why: A dependency graph tells the system which calculated values depend on the input.

questions.prompt: What makes NOW() and TODAY() different from ordinary formulas?
options: They depend on time, so a scheduler refreshes them
questions.why: These formulas change without record edits.

questions.prompt: How does the PDF describe revealing sensitive cells?
options: Allowlisted people reveal cells individually with logged reason
questions.why: Field-level controls require explicit reveal permissions and log the action.

modules.remember: Remember: a field is not just a column label; it has a codec, permissions, filter semantics and compute rules.

modules.title: 9. Query Engine and Grid Rendering
modules.overview: Follow how a browser view becomes a database query and why the grid avoids fetching the full table.

terms.definition: Logic translating view filters/sorts/search into SQL.
Paging with a position marker rather than large offsets.
Selecting only required columns/fields.
UI rendering only the visible subset of data.
Index-friendly typed representation of JSON values.
Update cached result from an incoming frame.
Display that groups records by a field.
Lightweight metadata sent for attachment cells.
Text indexing/querying across supported fields.

flow: Browser requests a table/view with filters, sorts, groupings and needed field IDs.
POST …/records/query compiles this into SQL over JSONB cells, typed sidecars and computed values.
Server returns cursor-paged records with only fields the grid needs.
Initial grid loads up to 1,200 rows, then requests more as user scrolls.
Attachment cells include initial files and count; long text shows 300-character preview.
Realtime frames patch existing rows; grid searches only fields visible in that view.
modules.example: Learning example: Sales Kanban filters Status = Open and orders by Due Date; query compiler pushes conditions into SQL with sidecar support. Grid shows loaded cards, not every DB record at once. Specific SQL syntax is illustrative.

questions.prompt: What operation does the grid use to query records?
questions.why: The documented API compiles filters, sorts and search into SQL.

questions.prompt: Why request only visible/needed fields?
options: Reduce response size and rendering cost
questions.why: Field projection reduces payload for wide tables.

questions.prompt: What prevents full refetch after every collaborator edit?
options: Browser patches cached rows using realtime frames
questions.why: The source describes realtime cache patching, not full refetch on every edit.

modules.remember: Remember: SQL handles filtering, cursor pages bound work, and realtime patches keep the grid current.

modules.title: 10. Attachment Storage and Signed Links
modules.overview: Understand the private-bucket lifecycle from upload to authorized browser access.

terms.definition: File associated with a TableOS record.
Service for storing binary objects with object keys.
Path-like name locating an object.
Storage whose objects are not public by default.
Time-limited cryptographically authorized object request.
Google Cloud Storage signature proving allowed URL parameters.
Smaller preview derived from an attachment.
Node.js image processing library.
Storage provider copies objects without browser re-upload.

flow: Client uploads through TableOS API; the system stores the object in private GCS.
The object key includes workspace/base/attachment/filename organization.
The API verifies the caller's access before redirecting to a signed V4 link.
The source says thumbnail links are valid around 1 hour and full file links 10 minutes, bounded by an at-most 2-hour issuance window.
GCS refuses changing signed object or extending signed expiry.
Sharp generates thumbnails; records reference attachments and variants.
modules.example: Source note: On 19 Nov 2026, the former shared bucket's 319,341 objects were copied server-side; call recordings referenced from records remained in the older ai-calls/ path. These are historical operations in the PDF, not instructions for current migration.

questions.prompt: Are TableOS attachment files publicly readable without checks?
options: No, access is checked before a short signed URL
questions.why: Objects are private; the API checks access and provides temporary signed links.

questions.prompt: Why are signed URLs short-lived?
options: To limit reuse after an authorized access decision
questions.why: The expiry limits the duration of delegated access.

questions.prompt: Can an attacker alter the object key inside an existing signed URL and keep it valid?
options: No, the provider validates the signature against the signed request
questions.why: Changing protected URL parameters invalidates its signature.

modules.remember: Remember: authorization at the API and cryptographic time-limited storage access are two separate controls.

modules.title: 11. Sync and External Integrations
modules.overview: Distinguish a copied synced table from ordinary-table HubSpot field mapping and understand conflict resolution.

terms.definition: Stored credential/config for an external provider.
Authenticated symmetric encryption algorithm.
Read-only mirror from another system into TableOS.
Fetch changes since previous checkpoint.
Re-fetch complete source for reconciliation.
Changes can flow in both directions.
terms.example: TableOS and HubSpot edit a deal.

terms.definition: Associating a TableOS field with a provider property.
Attribute used to pair records lacking stored IDs.
Choosing a value when both systems edited same field.
Last observed values/state saved for each side.
Buffered outbound updates to another system.
Proof Key for Code Exchange strengthening OAuth authorization code flow.
Locally stored provider field definitions.

flow: Owner configures encrypted organization-shared connection.
Synced table pulls another TableOS base, Airtable table, HubSpot object or Gmail inbox; it normally presents read-only copied data.
HubSpot field mapping instead links an ordinary table to provider object properties; each mapping has one of three directions.
Match records using stored HubSpot ID or configured match key; create unmatched records on the permitted side.
Compare saved per-side field values to see what changed; when both changed a two-way field, source says newer edit wins.
Run periodically (5–1,440 minutes), shortly after an edit, or manually; HubSpot properties refresh hourly. Source states deletes are not propagated.
modules.example: Learning example: Map local Deals.Amount ↔ HubSpot Deals.amount. TableOS becomes 500, HubSpot becomes 600 later, both since last sync; the latest change wins according to the documented policy. Record IDs and values are illustrative. This is not a proof of conflict-safety in all clock scenarios.

questions.prompt: Who manages organization-shared integration connections in the PDF?
questions.why: Connections are owner-managed and stored encrypted.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a synced table from HubSpot field mapping?
options: Synced table copies a source into a read-only table; mapping syncs selected fields on an ordinary table
questions.why: These are distinct integration features and workflows.

questions.prompt: What happens if both sides changed the same two-way mapped field?
options: Newer change wins under documented rule
questions.why: The document says newer change wins after tracking last values on each side.

modules.remember: Remember: shared connection → select source → pair records → compare changed fields → apply direction → update/checkpoint.

modules.title: 12. Automations, Interfaces and Sharing
modules.overview: Learn how automation triggers and steps execute durably, and why public experiences have limited tokens.

terms.definition: Condition starting a workflow.
Action within a workflow.
Persisted workflow run/step progress.
Repeated execution gives the same intended effect.
Check preventing automation from retriggering itself forever.
Short-lived identity for automation execution.
Page-based app over selected base data.
Tokenized access to a limited public view or form.
Bound on actions/requests in time.
Incoming HTTP event that starts an automation.

flow: Create automation trigger (record created/updated/matches, form, schedule, webhook or button).
Configure ordered actions (create/update records, email, Slack, webhook, script).
Store run/step state in Postgres and execute steps via BullMQ.
Guard against duplicate execution and loops; run in the owner's permission context.
Short-lived service session may access masked values for authorized operations; such reveal access is logged.
Public views/forms/interfaces use distinct share tokens and rate limits in the separate public app.
modules.example: Learning example: Ticket created → automation triggers → worker creates run record → sends Slack notification → marks step completed. If worker retries, idempotency should prevent duplicate notifications; exact implementation specifics beyond described guarantees are not given.

questions.prompt: Which can trigger a TableOS automation?
questions.why: The PDF lists record changes, form submissions, schedules, webhooks and buttons.

questions.prompt: Why store automation run and step state in PostgreSQL?
options: To make execution durable and inspectable
questions.why: Persisted states survive worker interruptions and support retries.

questions.prompt: An automation updates the same field that triggers itself repeatedly. What guards against runaway execution?
questions.why: Loop guards are explicitly documented for automation safety.

modules.remember: Remember: trigger → durable run → queued steps → owner-scoped execution → idempotent completion.

modules.title: 13. Security, Roles and Access
modules.overview: Understand layered authentication and authorization without confusing organization account type, base role and field visibility.

terms.definition: Organization-wide level: Owner, Admin or Member.
Resource-scoped permissions: Owner, Creator, Editor, Commenter, Read only, Interface only or No access.
Credential representing signed-in browser session.
Credential sent in Authorization header.
One-way digest used instead of storing raw bearer token.
Set of allowed operations/resources.
Time-based one-time password factor.
Owner approval for a browser device to access an organization.
Fine-grained control of field editing/reveal.
Return obscured values until authorized reveal.
Owner-only high-privilege API token reaching all bases and sensitive fields.
Time-limited join link stored protected.
Recorded security-relevant action.

flow: Request authenticates using browser session or bearer API token.
MFA, forced password change and approved device policy are enforced at authentication boundary.
Account type plus workspace/base roles and grants produce compiled access snapshot.
Route checks a specific action; field edit and sensitive reveal rules add finer checks.
Owner alone manages Members & access and Connectors; Admin has operational powers but not those settings.
API tokens have scopes, base restrictions, expiry and rate limits; logged calls and revocation are documented.
modules.example: Example (illustrative): a Member has Editor role in the Support base but No access to Finance. The compiled snapshot allows record.update in Support only. The document also describes owner-only master-token behavior including unmask, and that such tokens stop when the creator loses Owner status.

questions.prompt: Who can manage organization connectors according to the PDF?
questions.why: Owner alone manages connections and connector settings.

questions.prompt: Does having organization Admin status automatically grant access to every base?
options: No, Admin opens only bases it has been granted
questions.why: The table says Owners have all; Admins and Members have 'given' base access.

questions.prompt: What happens to an owner's master token after its creator is no longer an Owner?
options: It becomes a public share link
It changes to a TOTP code
questions.why: The source explicitly states master token rights depend on the creator retaining Owner status.

modules.remember: Remember: identity → organization account type → workspace/base role → specific action → field-level rules.

modules.title: 14. History, Undo, Trash and Audit
modules.overview: Distinguish ordinary record history from recoverable deletion and organization-wide security audit.

terms.definition: Persisted record-change version.
terms.example: Status changed from Open to Done.

terms.definition: Ability to reverse or reapply prior edits.
Saved group of deleted items for restoration.
Scheduled permanent removal of expired trash items.
Policy defining how long history or trash is kept.
Security event log for accountability.
PostgreSQL table of security-relevant actions.
Per-record list of changes.

flow: Each record edit writes a record_revisions entry.
Users can view record activity and use per-base undo/redo, including after page reload.
Deleted records are tracked in deletion_batches so they can be restored from trash.
Schedulers enforce retention and purge eligible trash.
Security-relevant actions write to audit.audit_events rather than being mixed with ordinary row history.
modules.example: Learning scenario: An editor deletes a customer record, then restores it from Trash. The record's ordinary changes belong in record_revisions; a security-setting change belongs in audit.audit_events. Which exact data is retained depends on platform retention policy not enumerated in the source.

questions.prompt: Which table records ordinary record revisions?
questions.why: Record history lives in data.record_revisions.

questions.prompt: Where are deleted records tracked for restoration?
questions.why: Deletion batches represent recoverable trash.

questions.prompt: How do record history and security audit differ?
options: Revisions describe record edits; audit_events describe security-relevant actions
questions.why: They serve separate accountability needs.

modules.remember: Remember: revisions = data history; deletion batches = trash; audit_events = security activity.

modules.title: 15. Operations, Releases and Limits
modules.overview: Know how TableOS is tested, released, deployed and monitored, and distinguish deployed limits from planned scaling.

terms.definition: Branch holding a prepared version release.
Static TypeScript validation.
Test that old behavior still works after changes.
Browser automation framework.
API applies outstanding schema migrations when launched.
Machine-readable request/event logs.
Latency below which 95% of measured requests fall.
Operational charts for metrics.
terms.example: CPU, memory, latency and DB health.

terms.definition: Documented product/infrastructure bound.
Partitioning data across multiple database instances.
Human sign-off before merging a release.
terms.example: Merge to master only after approval.

flow: Develop changes on a feature branch and test locally with dummy data.
Run type checks, server build, regression scripts and Playwright UI check with screenshots.
Bump version; push release/vX.Y.Z to complete remote.
Merge approved release to master; Render deploys master.
API applies missing migrations on startup; deployment restarts API, realtime, worker and relay.
Observe Grafana metrics and Render pino JSON logs; investigate incidents using request status and timing.
modules.example: As built limits (19 Nov 2026): one PostgreSQL and one Redis/Valkey instance for all tenants; each synced table up to 50,000 records; incremental HubSpot search capped at 10,000 changes before a full read; HubSpot field mapping does not propagate deletes. These are source-dated statements.

modules.example: Interview script: 'TableOS is a multi-tenant relational workspace product with flexible JSONB record storage. Fastify handles authenticated requests; changes commit with revisions, base changes and an outbox. Redis/Valkey distributes realtime and jobs; a relay publishes durable events; workers handle search, automation and sync. Private GCS stores files. The current deployment uses a single Postgres/Redis; sharding is a future target.'
